Research.Basket.Title: Fund Basket
Research.Basket.Hint: Pick up to five tracked funds to view together. Nothing is saved: the basket lives in this page's address.
Research.Basket.SearchLabel: Add a fund to the basket
Research.Sectors.Lean.Title: Lean vs the market
Research.Sectors.TechNote: Lights SEC's Technology office plus computer hardware and semiconductor makers (SIC 3570–3579 and 3670–3679), which SEC reviews under Manufacturing.
Research.Sectors.OfficesHint: Choose an office to zoom into it.
Research.Sectors.BasketAbout1: Your basket view adds up each fund's holdings from its latest Form N-PORT report, weighted by the fund's share of your basket. Every percent is of your basket, counting stocks, bonds and cash.
Research.Sectors.BasketAbout2: Each stock is matched to an SEC filer by company name and grouped by that filer's SEC industry office and SIC industry. Foreign companies that file no reports with the SEC have no SEC industry, and a few companies match no SEC filer by name (often ones renamed or delisted since the report), so they are shown hatched grey under "Not classified by the SEC", by the country where each issuer is organized. Shares of other funds count as cash and other. Each industry lists its ten largest companies; the rest are summed into "Other".
Research.Sectors.MarketAbout1: Public float is the market value of a company's shares held by investors other than its insiders, as the company reports it once a year to the SEC. It leaves out insiders' holdings, so it is smaller than the company's total value, and it changes only once a year.
Research.Sectors.MarketAbout2: Only US SEC filers are included, so small companies and some foreign companies (those filing annual reports on Form 20-F) are missing. Each company is grouped by the SEC office that reviews its filings and by its SIC industry code.
Research.Source.NportReturns: Source: SEC EDGAR (Form N-PORT monthly total returns)
Research.Funds.Overlap.Title: Overlap: same holdings
Research.Funds.Overlap.Subtitle: How much of two funds' money is in the same securities, from each fund's latest reported holdings ({dates}). For each security both funds hold, the smaller of its two weights is counted, and those are added up.
Research.Funds.Overlap.Prompt: Add at least two funds to your Fund Basket to see how much they overlap.
Research.Funds.Overlap.Note: Each fund's label filters the table to the holdings that fund shares; pointing at or focusing a cell highlights that pair's holdings. The table is built from the 25 largest holdings each pair shares. With three or more funds, the share held by two or more is a lower bound.
Research.Funds.Correlation.Title: Correlation: move together
Research.Funds.Correlation.Subtitle: How closely two funds' monthly returns rose and fell together over the window: 1 is fully in step, 0 is unrelated and −1 is opposite. From monthly total returns of each fund's net asset value, to {month}.
Research.Funds.Correlation.Prompt: Add at least two funds to your Fund Basket, or choose All tracked funds, to see how closely they move together.
Research.Funds.Correlation.Note: Each value is the Pearson correlation of the two funds' monthly returns over the window's months, ending with the earlier of their latest months. It describes how they moved in the past only. A dash means a fund has too few months for the window.
Research.Funds.Holdings.Title: What the tracked funds hold
Research.Funds.HowToReadText: Each circle's size follows its share of the fund's net assets. A filled circle has more inside it; use Enter or Space on a focused item to open or close it, and the arrow keys to move between items.
Research.Funds.About1: Funds report their holdings to the SEC on Form N-PORT. The reports for the last month of each fiscal quarter are public, so the holdings are quarterly snapshots, not daily, and are published some weeks after the date they are as of.
Research.Funds.About2: Shares are of each fund's net assets. Vanguard's ETFs are share classes of larger Vanguard funds, so their figures are for the whole fund. Derivatives can show a small negative share.
Research.Source.Performance: Sources: SEC EDGAR (Form N-PORT monthly total returns). Inflation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, CPI-U. Interest rates: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, H.15 Selected Interest Rates.
Research.Source.Risk: Sources: SEC EDGAR (Form N-PORT monthly total returns and net assets; Form N-CSR expense ratios). Treasury bill rate: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, H.15 Selected Interest Rates.
Research.Performance.Title: Growth of 100
Research.Performance.Subtitle: How 100 put into your basket and into each of its funds would have grown, from each fund's monthly total return on its net asset value, with distributions reinvested. The basket is rebalanced to its weights every month.
Research.Performance.RealMissing: The inflation data has not loaded yet, so only nominal values are shown.
Research.Performance.Prompt: Add funds to your Fund Basket to see how they grew.
Research.Performance.Keys: Use the left and right arrow keys to move through the months, Home and End for the first and last.
Research.Performance.BrushLabel: Drag across the strip to choose the period; the buttons set it too
Research.Performance.HowToRead1: Every line starts at 100 at the end of the month before the first month all your funds have a return. A line at 150 means 100 grew to 150. "Your basket" is the heavier dark line.
Research.Performance.HowToRead2: Adjusted for inflation divides each line by how much consumer prices rose since the start, so it shows growth in buying power. A month the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish (October 2025, during the government shutdown) is filled in between the months either side.
Research.Performance.HowToRead3: The lower panels share the chart's months: the effective federal funds rate, and your basket minus the fund you compare it with, in points of the growth of 100 (blue where the basket is ahead, orange where it is behind). Drag across the strip under the chart, or use the period buttons, to zoom; every line then starts at 100 again and the figures cover that period.
Research.Performance.About1: Funds report a total return for each month on Form N-PORT. These are returns on the fund's net asset value at month ends, not market prices, and they are published some weeks after the quarter they cover.
Research.Performance.About2: The figures describe the past only; they say nothing about what will happen.
Research.Risk.Subtitle: Each fund's annualized return against its volatility, how much its monthly returns swung (as a yearly figure), over the window. Bubble area follows the fund's net assets; your basket is the dark diamond.
Research.Risk.FactsMissing: The fund facts have not loaded yet, so every bubble has the same size.
Research.Risk.PanelLabel: About the risk and return data
Research.Risk.HowToRead1: Higher up means a higher annualized return over the window; further right means bigger swings from month to month. No part of the chart is better than another: it shows how the funds behaved, not what to choose.
Research.Risk.HowToRead2: The dashed lines cross at your basket, so each corner reads against it: higher or lower return, smaller or bigger swings than your basket over the window.
Research.Risk.HowToRead3: The Sharpe ratio is the return above the 3-month Treasury bill rate for each point of volatility. It is negative when a fund returned less than the bill.
Research.Risk.About: Returns are on each fund's net asset value at month ends, from Form N-PORT. Expense ratios are from each fund's latest shareholder report; SPY, a unit investment trust, files none with machine-readable figures.

Research.World.Title: Stock-market value by country
Research.World.Subtitle: Market capitalisation of listed domestic companies in {period}, by country.
Research.World.About1: Market capitalisation is the share price times the number of shares of the companies listed on a country's stock exchanges, at the end of each year, in current US dollars. The World Bank publishes it from the World Federation of Exchanges.
Research.World.About2: % of GDP compares it with the size of the country's economy in the same year. Countries without a stock exchange, or that do not report, show as "No data".
Research.WorldBasket.Title: Your basket by issuer country
Research.WorldBasket.Subtitle: Where your basket's holdings are, weighted by your funds' shares. Countries are where each holding's issuer is organized, as each fund reports it; currency is what each holding is priced in, so American depositary receipts (ADRs) count as US dollars. This is not where companies earn their revenue. From each fund's latest holdings report ({dates}).
Research.WorldBasket.Prompt: Add funds to your Fund Basket to see where its holdings are.
Research.WorldBasket.HowToRead: Each country's colour is its share of your basket. The scale tops out at the largest country outside the US, so the rest of the world stays readable; the US always takes the darkest step, and its true share is in its tooltip. Small places the map cannot draw, such as Hong Kong and Singapore, are dots sized by their share. Shares under 0.05% read "<0.1%".
Research.WorldBasket.About: Funds report each holding's issuer country and currency on Form N-PORT. Funds follow their own conventions: the same company can have a different country in different funds, and American depositary receipts count as US dollars. Securities-lending collateral is left out, and cash not reported as a holding is unallocated.

Research.Companies.About1: Every figure is as the company reported it to the SEC in its annual reports (Form 10-K, or 20-F and 40-F for some foreign companies), in US dollars under US accounting rules (US GAAP). A restated figure replaces the original.
Research.Companies.About2: There are no share prices, market values or recommendations here. A figure the company did not report in this form shows as "Not reported", never as zero, and nothing is converted from another currency.
Research.Companies.About3: Margins and growth are worked out from the reported figures. They show as "Not shown" when a figure is missing or when the base is zero or negative. Liabilities include anything the company does not report as equity.
Research.Companies.About4: Banks and insurers often report revenue differently, so their revenue may be missing. Shares outstanding and Public float are taken from the cover of each annual report.
